title: Low strength and a shared size distribution connect the hot and cold Kuiper belt populations

paper_content.abstract: Understanding how the observed size distribution of Kuiper Belt objects emerged from the primordial planetesimal population remains a major challenge in planetary science. In particular, the similarity between the size distributions of dynamically hot and cold populations in the 100–400 km range calls for a unified explanation. Motivated by this observational constraint and by theoretical models of pebble accretion, we model the coupled dynamical and collisional evolution of the trans-planetary disc under the early instability scenario. Here we show that a common planetesimal formation mechanism operating up to about 400 km and modulated by an exponential taper shape, combined with a transition to a shallow power law distribution in the inner disc, can reproduce the current size-frequency distributions of cold and hot populations. This outcome requires assuming that planetesimals were weaker to impacts than previously thought. Our results connect formation models with current observations, thereby constraining the early conditions of the Solar System and the properties of planetesimals.
paper_content.introduction:
The inventory of dynamically hot and cold Kuiper belt objects (KBOs) has been proposed to be nearly complete for objects with absolute magnitude H r < 5.3, and this has been confirmed by dedicated surveys. The achievement of near completeness in that magnitude range opens new possibilities to better constrain the early Solar System after the gas dispersal phase.

The Outer Solar System Origins Survey (OSSOS), along with following extensions referred to as OSSOS++, provides a comprehensive debiased sample of dynamically hot and cold Kuiper belt (KB) populations (hereinafter HKB and CKB, respectively), together with their absolute magnitude H r distribution. Supported by such surveys, the H r distribution of the cold classical population was found to be accurately approximated by an exponentially tapered function in H r ≃ 5 to 12 range. Later findings indicate that the absolute magnitude distributions of dynamically hot and cold populations in the 5.5 < H r < 8.3 range (corresponding roughly to 100–400 km diameter range) are essentially indistinguishable. Such observational evidence provided by OSSOS++ contradicts the previously prevailing view, when it was widely accepted that the cumulative size-frequency distributions (SFD) of the hot and cold components of the KB were well described by broken power laws of the form N(>D) ∝ Dq, where N(>D) is the number of objects with diameter larger than D, and q is the cumulative slope of the distribution. Specifically, at the large-size end (D > 100 km), the cold component was thought to have a steeper slope (q cold = −7.5) than the hot component (q hot = −4.5). The evidence provided by has posed a challenge to the previous notion that the primordial Kuiper belt displayed different SFDs slopes in its inner and outer regions, implying different formation processes.

The general understanding of the outer solar system dynamical evolution is encompassed under the umbrella of the new Nice model. According to this model, the planetesimals surrounding the giant planets, remaining after their formation, were located in a disc extending about 22 to 30 au, with an estimated mass about 30 M⊕. As dynamical instability ensued, the influence of Neptune played a significant role in depleting that disc. Most of the mass was dispersed at very large heliocentric distance, while some bodies were implanted in the current region of Plutinos, and others eventually found their way to the HKB.

There is a consensus on the hypothesis that the cold population, with a current mass of about 10−3 M⊕, was born in situ and remained primordial, based on the large fraction of binaries still in the CKB and their distinctive red colours. This argument was later reinforced by the New Horizons images of Arrokoth, showing scarcity of craters on its surface, suggesting that collisional evolution did not significantly alter the primordial SFD of that population. Based on measurements by OSSOS++, it has been suggested that the SFD of the cold and hot components may have maintained their primordial shape for objects in the size range of about 100–400 km. Accordingly, the same mechanism responsible for the accretion of bodies in their primordial formation region might be common to both populations.

As far as planetesimal growth is concerned, the streaming instability (SI) model gives valuable insights into the initial phase of planetesimal formation by providing an efficient and fast mechanism for growing planetesimals from dust particles or pebble clumps within protoplanetary discs. The SI is an aerodynamic process driven by the velocity difference between solid particles and gas and the reaction of solids onto the gas. This mechanism led to the formation of high-density regions, providing a favourable environment for gravitational collapse and subsequent aggregation into planetesimals.

Lyra et al. found that considering a pebble size distribution in the accretion process (also refereed as polydisperse pebble accretion) following SI was critical in planetesimal formation. According to this study, such a process was responsible for accretion of up to a few hundred km (about 300–400 km) at heliocentric distances as far as the current location of the CKB. This finding is essential in defining a common formation mechanism for the primordial trans–planetary populations (between 22 and 30 au) and the cold population of bodies up to such size, confirming previous conjectures. According to accretion models, further growth strongly depends on mass conditions at different heliocentric distances. This is the reason why accretion to Pluto (and possibly larger) size bodies was efficient in the inner region between 22 and 30 au. Instead, beyond 40 au, planetesimals should have remained as such, as further accretion was prevented by low mass density conditions in the nebula.

The inventory of large bodies in the Kuiper belt seems nowadays relatively complete for H r < 5.3, while the SFD of fainter (smaller) bodies remains largely incomplete. Valuable insights into impactor SFD and collisional processes are achieved by exploring planetary surface impact craters. Thus, the surfaces of Pluto and Charon offer a unique opportunity to examine the crater population in the outer solar system. Robins et al. provide results that reconcile earlier discrepancies in the estimated crater size distribution slopes obtained from the New Horizons fly-by of both worlds. They estimate that the size distribution of small craters has a shallower slope than for large ones, consistent with previously reported results by Singer et al. (hereinafter S19). Nevertheless, according to the authors, the crater size-frequency distribution slopes are uncertain, in particular at small sizes. In fact, slope values for craters below 10–15 km is −0.7 ± 0.2, and −2.8 ± 0.6 for larger craters; implying a deficit of small KBOs below 1–2 km. Such estimated slopes are very sensitive to the choice of parameters and the craters used in the statistical analysis, and they must be taken as minima in the uncertainty determination. On the other hand, Morbidelli et al. (hereinafter M21) established a connection between their re-examined Pluto and Charon cratering record and Arrokoth’s cratering record, including the dust measurement (down to 2 μm approximately) obtained from the New Horizons space mission by NASA. Their findings revealed that the SFD shows a moderate decline below 2 km, which contrasts with the claim made by S19 of an exceedingly shallow slope. In addition, M21 argue that the shallow portion of the SFD extends to around 30 m before transitioning to a steeper slope to match the dust abundance constraint.

Collisional models are commonly used to study small body populations evolution in the solar system. However, since the adoption of the new Nice model framework, only two studies have examined the collisional evolution of the trans-planetary disc in detail. First, Asteroid-LIke Collisional And Dynamical Evolution Package (ALICANDEP-22) was applied to conduct a systematic study exploring different initial distributions for the trans–planetary disc and different scaling laws that govern the impact response. They got a good match with available observational evidence when it was still thought that the CKB and HKB had different SFD slopes at the bright end. Later, the Boulder code was applied to study the collisional evolution of the primordial KB and other related populations as the destabilised population and the Jupiter Trojans. The main constraints used in the latter include the size distributions of the Trojan asteroids and craters on the giant planets satellites.

The presence of Pluto-sized and larger bodies in the hot population implies that the initial SFD of the inner trans-planetary disc must have extended beyond 400 km. Moreover, theoretical studies of planetesimal accretion suggest that, in the inner disc, a power law tail likely developed with a relatively shallow slope, enabling the growth of several thousand dwarf planets. When combined with an exponentially tapered distribution, characteristic of the cold population, this configuration provides a natural explanation for the properties of the hot and cold Kuiper Belt populations within a unified formation framework.

Here we show that the observed SFDs of both dynamically hot and cold Kuiper Belt populations can be reproduced by modelling their collisional and dynamical evolution from a common primordial distribution. We adopt an initial SFD shaped by a shared formation mechanism up to 400 km, transitioning to a shallow power law tail in the inner disc, and evolve it under the early instability scenario. Our simulations indicate that matching current observations requires assuming low material strength for planetesimals.
paper_content.results:
Outline of the model
We modelled the KB collisional and dynamical evolution using the ALICANDEP-22 package. This model simulates collisional evolution within the framework of the current interpretation of the Nice model for the dynamical evolution of the outer solar system. Dynamical evolution is carried out through statistical elimination of bodies from an inner disc and implantation into the current KB. The modelled scenario begins with the initial mass concentrated in an inner disc (outside Neptune’s orbit), ranging from 22 to 30 au. We also considered a small concentration of mass between 42 and 47 au, standing for the in-situ formation of the cold classical population. The initial population born in the inner disc undergoes three evolution phases, including collisional and dynamical evolution processes such as excitation, migration, and mass depletion. Each phase consists of the following features. Phase 1: We call this the pre-instability phase, lasting from time t 0 to t i. It denotes the onset of Neptune’s outward migration as it enters the inner disc. This phase results in an increase in eccentricity and inclination of planetesimals. Such dynamical excitation increased relative velocities (see “Methods”) and, therefore, the overall collisional evolution. Additionally, some smooth mass-loss during this period—according to dynamical models—is also included. Phase 2: This period is known as the instability phase. In our model, it lasts from t i to t i + Δt. In this phase, Neptune passed through the inner disc, which led to minor collisional evolution and significant dynamical depletion. During this time, most planetesimals were ejected from the solar system; some were removed inwards, while others were implanted into the excited Kuiper belt populations. Phase 3: This is the post-instability phase, lasting from t i + Δt to the end of the simulations (4500 Myr). At the beginning of this phase, the inner disc was already depleted, and the outer regions corresponding to Plutinos and hot classical belt populations were populated. Negligible collisional evolution took place in this phase.

In ALICANDEP-22, the outer region of the solar system is divided into three zones, representing different Kuiper belt populations: Plutinos, cold classicals, and hot classicals. The collisional evolution of each zone is performed taking into account mutual interaction between different zones. The orbital elements, semi-major axis (a), eccentricity (e) and inclination (i) of the inner zone and the three outer zones for each dynamical phase, are shown in Table 1. For the instability onset we tested t i = 10 to 100 Myr, with Δt = 10 and 30 Myr.

Regarding the response of bodies to impacts, numerical studies tend to shift from 200 m to around 20 m, the size at which scaling laws for the threshold specific energy for disruption (Q* D) have a minimum. This was first suggested to suitably fit the cratering record on Pluto, Charon, and Arrokoth, and to explain the survival of the satellite of the Trojan asteroid Eurybates (Queta). Moreover, a study on collisional evolution of the primordial Kuiper belt, its destabilised population, and the Trojans asteroids, also finds that such scaling laws produce better results to match the Trojan asteroids populations and the crater distributions on giant planets satellites. Further details about the implementation of scaling laws are presented in the Methods section.

The initial SFD is an essential boundary condition in the progress of populations of systems under moderate collisional evolution. In such systems, as in the case of the Kuiper belt, the SFD slopes for large bodies are not modified along the evolution; thus, their features must be primordial. Accordingly, we must reproduce the gradual transition towards larger bodies currently observed in the SFD of the implanted hot component. Therefore, we propose that the initial population in the inner trans–planetary region combines a tapered distribution up to D tr about 100–400 km, with a decreasing power law distribution for D > D tr. Such population contained around of 4000 Pluto–size (and larger) bodies. Two values were tested for D tr: 100 and 400 km. In the case of the primordial cold disc, an SFD identical in shape to the inner disc but with much less mass—and no population of bodies larger than 400 km—was chosen as the initial distribution, following the planetesimal formation mechanisms discussed above. At the small-size end, the cumulative H r magnitude distribution is governed by an exponent α s (see “Methods,” subsection Initial size distribution). In the following section, we show results for primordial distributions with α s values of 0.4 and 0.3, which are our steep and shallow distributions (see “Methods,” subsection Model flexibility to match observational uncertainties, for a detailed exploration of the initial SFD parameters). The total mass of the primordial population is approximately 30 M⊕, assuming an average bulk density of 1000 kg/m3.

Observational constraints
The main constraint in this study comes from the debiased magnitude distribution of the hot and cold populations provided by updated surveys. The OSSOS++ team graciously provided us with the magnitude distribution of each component, making this task easier. Due to the fact that the OSSOS++ survey may overestimate the size distribution of bright bodies, we preferred to use the Minor Planet Center (MPC) database for the distribution of bodies with H r ≲ 5.5. Several pencil-beam surveys have been conducted to identify faint Kuiper belt objects. Bernstein et al. used the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to measure the faintest Kuiper belt objects for which a direct SFD can be obtained. They detected three CKB bodies and none in the HKB population. Kavelaars et al. debiased the three detections in the cold population using the same procedure as for OSSOS++. This estimation is also used in this work as an observational constraint. In the Methods section, we utilize observational uncertainties to investigate the flexibility of the model while ensuring it remains consistent with the range of possible SFD permitted by the OSSOS++ data, including the debiased estimation by Bernstein et al.

We assumed the average albedo of each population (p r = 0.15 and 0.08 for cold and hot KBOs, respectively) for size conversion. Both tested transition sizes D tr = 100 and 400 km provide satisfactory results; however, we centred our analysis on the case corresponding to D tr = 100 km, because it best matched the constraint of a smooth slope transition in the 100–400 km size range to larger bodies. In the subsection Considerations on the Kuiper Belt Populations, two additional constraints are discussed: the change in the SFD slope at 1–2 km and the Jupiter trojans SFD slope for 5–100 km size bodies.

Model outcome
Figure 1 shows the model outcome of the cumulative SFD for the hot and cold populations after 4500 Myr of evolution. For comparison, the SFD corresponding to the debiased absolute magnitude distribution for each dynamical population is also shown along with the corresponding Poisson 95% confidence range estimated by the OSSOS++. Different scaling laws were tested, showing that the final distributions, for large bodies, are not very sensitive to the very values of the scaling law for shattering (Q* S), provided that we choose a weak one and that the minimum value of the distribution is about 20 m (see “Methods,” subsection Impact outcome).

Hot classical population
The match between the modelled hot classical population and the debiased distribution is excellent, particularly in the size range from about 70 to 400 km. For larger bodies, the modelled SFD follows the MPC database, essentially complete at this size range. Nevertheless, for completeness, we also explore the uncertainty range of the OSSOS++ survey (see Methods, subsection Model flexibility to match observational uncertainties).

The hot classical population was born in a massive disc, though with low relative velocities due to small values of eccentricity and inclination. That circumstance only allowed fair collisional grinding down to about 20 km. However, at sizes below 100 km, a moderate wavy behaviour in the SFD can be noticed, in the case where the weakest scaling law is assumed (solid blue line in Fig. 1a). Collisional grinding appears then subtle, and the very characteristics of each fragmentation scaling law leave minor fingerprints in the evolved SFD, even when delaying the onset of instability from 10 to 100 Myr (see Methods, subsection Time dependence). The shift of the minima in the scaling laws down to some 20 m is crucial in the propagation of the wavy pattern, even at large sizes (about 10 km).

Cold classical population
Agreement of our results with the debiased distribution is very accurate for the cold component across the comparable size range (70 < D < 400 km). That is particularly evident when the assumed initial distribution has a steep slope at the small–size end (α s = 0.4), as is observed today. Further simulations constrain the possible values of α s in the range of 0.27 to 0.42 to be consistent with the error bar of the debiased estimation of the faintest detected objects in the CKB (black error bar in Fig. 1b). The uncertainties of the OSSOS++ also allow a modest variation in the slope of the taper function at large sizes. The threshold values defining the initial SFD are explored in the Methods section.

Negligible collisional evolution took place in this region, and the final distribution is a slightly depleted version of the primordial one. ALICANDEP-22 can keep track of the amount of objects that are disrupted, or just shattered and gravitationally re-aggregated. In this way, we find that—in the cold classical population—bodies larger than about 1–10 km are expected to be primordial and to have experienced only cratering events, even in the case the weakest shattering scaling law is considered in our model. Consequently, their dynamically relaxed initial conditions strongly support that this population was preserved in its primordial state due to negligible collisional evolution. This confirms findings indicating that Arrokoth is most likely a primordial body.

Considerations on the Kuiper Belt populations
It has been pointed out in the literature that the KBO SFD exhibits distinctive features. First, a break at 100 km referred to as the “knee” was found, where the cumulative slope transitions from steeper to shallower. Also, a secondary break at about D = 1–2 km, known as the “elbow,” was suggested, where the slope shifts from a value in the range of −2.8 to −3.2 to an even shallower slope with a corresponding q in the range of −0.7 to −1.2, in terms of cumulative distribution (see Introduction). We find that an exponential taper shape SFD of the primordial population, below 100–400 km, easily reproduces the knee at about 100 km, as shown in Fig. 1, for the hot and cold dynamical population, and in Fig. 2 for the total KB population (Plutinos, HKB, and CKB).

The transition region between the knee and the elbow (2 < D < 100 km) must follow a cumulative SFD slope similar to the one observed in the captured population of Jupiter Trojans (q ~ −2), described by the red dotted line in Fig. 2. We faithfully reproduce such behaviour in all the simulations adopting a steep slope (α s = 0.4) for the current H magnitude distribution. In contrast, beginning the evolution with a shallower slope (α s = 0.3), implies that the final SFD will also be shallower than expected in that transition size range. This is due to the fact that collisional evolution is unable to increase the slope to the one expected for Jupiter Trojans. We show this in Fig. 2, highlighting the need for the chosen slope (α s = 0.4) to meet observational constraints.

The behaviour of the SFD in the vicinity of the elbow deserves closer examination. Following previous studies on crater counts on Pluto and Charon, we consider the impact record estimated for Vulcan Planitia on Charon in S19, as it may best represent the primary population of impactors. Therefore, we obtained the nominal impactor SFD and plotted it along with the outcome of our model (Fig. 2) by suitably scaling it to the Kuiper belt distribution.

The model that best agrees with the predicted impactor population of cratering record estimations features a steep initial slope (α s = 0.4) and the weakest scaling law. This is represented by the solid blue line in Fig. 2. The match is remarkable in the 0.7–10 km size range, approximately. The S19 impactor distribution at smaller sizes instead bends over along a shallower slope. There is limited data availability in the sub-kilometer size range, so uncertainties related to crater count are relevant. Figure 2b shows the elbow size range in detail, including uncertainty estimation within 2σ (for small bodies), using as a reference the number of impactors corresponding to about D = 1.5 km, where the distribution gradually changes its slope. Our best matching case reproduces fairly well the gradual slope change (between 1 and 2 km) confirmed by crater count, while for smaller bodies it is close to the upper 2σ slope uncertainty, for the estimated distribution of impactors. For completeness, the cumulative distribution estimated by M21 is also plotted in Fig. 2b. The slope of the SFD corresponding to M21 model is similar to that found in our study in the 0.1–1 km size range, except for their underestimated population (by a factor about 3) below 1 km. Given the uncertainties in slope estimation of the crater size distribution, mainly due to the smooth transition from large to small craters, S19 and M21 estimations are not necessarily at odds with each other, and our model seem to be compatible with both interpretations within uncertainty limits.

In any case, we find that the only way to reproduce the elbow is to assume a weak strength for bodies in the primordial trans–planetary disc. This finding is in agreement with the 2023 study by Bottke et al. of collisional evolution based on current Trojan asteroids SFD and giant planets satellites cratering data, requiring a similar scaling law to be matched. Thus, despite the relatively small influence of collisional evolution, restricted to an early phase and constrained by the onset of the early solar system dynamical depletion, it is still significant in producing a bump at 1–2 km and propagating the wavy shape up to 10 km in the evolved SFD. Observational efforts are imperative for improving our comprehension of sub-kilometre outer solar system bodies and refining our understanding of the distinctive features characterising such population.

While the SFD estimated by M21 broadly corresponds to our overall final SFD in the approximate size range of 2–100 km, differences show up at smaller sizes, particularly around 30 m, where the slope turns steep in M21. In our model, the transition to a steep slope occurs at about 100 m, rather than at 30 m. Therefore, M21 underestimate the total number of bodies in the 10−2 < D < 1 km range, compared to our results. At the smallest size end (D < 10−3 km), both models tend to converge to the steady state slope. An explanation for such discrepancy may be that their estimation of the total SFD is derived from the impact cratering record of bodies associated with different dynamical populations, such as Pluto and Charon (in the plutinos 3:2 mean motion resonance region), and Arrokoth (CKB). The key difference in our model, compared to M21’s, is the ability to follow the collisional evolution of individual populations, including their mutual interactions, resulting in accurate outcome of the end–state overall populations.
paper_content.methods:
The collisional model used in this work consists of two main components. One takes care of determining the impact outcome of any collision, the other one handles the collisional evolution, using the output of the first component as input to iterate the evolution of a given initial population over 4500 Myr. The entire code package is named ALICANDEP-22 and was fully described and tested in. We provide here some details that may help understanding the model outcomes described in this work.

Impact outcome
To model the impact outcome of any collision, we use the fragmentation and re-accumulation model by Petit & Farinella, with further improvements. This part of the package computes the number of fragments produced in any possible collision between objects of different size (mass) bins, considering a given scaling law for shattering (Q* S). Q* S is the threshold specific energy required to break a given mass body into a spectrum of single fragments, the largest one having exactly half the mass of the original target. Instead, Q* D is the specific energy required to disperse half of the mass of a given target. This is usually estimated from the outcome of smoothed-particle hydrodynamics codes. It is important to note that Q* D and Q* S are equal in the strength regime (small bodies), where no self–compression nor fragment re-accumulation takes place, but they are different in the gravity regime (large bodies). Studies suggest that KBOs and Jupiter Trojans—likely a captured population of the initial inner disc—may be very weak, with a minimum of the Q* D scaling law at 20 m. The fragmentational algorithm is based on the specific shattering energy (Q* S). This allows the estimation of the fraction of re-accumulated mass by self—gravity, a distinctive feature of the model. We reformulated the usual Q* D expression following de Elia and Brunini as:

Q* D = C 1 D^λ 1 [1 + C 2 D^λ 2] (1)

where C 1, C 2, λ 1, λ 2 correspond to the coefficients. Using the values expected for scaling law for icy bodies corresponding to an average impact speed of 3 km/s.

Then, from the parametric expression eq. (1), corresponding expression for Q* S is obtained.

Q* S = C 1 D^λ 1 [1 + C 2 D^λ 2] (2)

In this expression, changing the values of C 2 and λ 2 the corresponding Q* S can be changed. C 2 and λ 2 are parameters shaping the scaling law in the gravity regime. We use C 1 = 1.55, λ 1 = 0.36, C 2 = 8, and λ 2 = 1.8, to get our nominal Q* S scaling law, in agreement with Marschall et al. Thus, Q* S and Q* D overlap in the strength regime, and differ as expected in the gravity regime (see black and blue dot-dashed lines in (Fig. 3a). In our simulations, we also test two alternative scaling laws, obtained by scaling the nominal one up and down by a factor of 10 (Fig. 3a), to check the sensitivity of collisional evolution on the adopted scaling law.

Initial size-frequency distribution
Our study aims to build a common primordial SFD for the cold and inner discs for bodies up to a given size. The following methodology was used to build up such initial population. Assuming that the cold classical population retains its primordial SFD, as supported by the estimation of the magnitude distribution (N(<H r)), by Kavelaars et al., we build up the cold population starting from the following relationship:

N(<H r) = N c1 10^α s (H r − H 0) exp [−10^β(H r − H B)] (3)

where N(<H r) is the population of bodies with absolute magnitude less than H r. Parameter values are: H 0 = −2.6, α s = 0.4, β = 0.25 and H B = 8.1, from Petit et al., and N c1 is a constant value. To estimate the mass, we assumed an average albedo, p r = 0.15, typical of the cold population, and bulk density ρ = 1000 kg m−3, resulting in a total initial mass M 0 cold = 1.3 × 10−3 M⊕. In this way, we also obtain the primordial SFD for that region with one largest body of about 375 km in size.

To build up the distribution of the inner population, we use the same functional form as for the cold SFD, but scaled up to obtain a suitable larger mass by several orders of magnitude. Such function extends the distribution up to about D = 800 km size bodies, due to the first term in Eq. (4), supported by streaming instability simulations. Such distribution need to be combined with a population of even larger bodies so that the SFD must be extended to larger sizes (dwarf planets and beyond) in the inner disc. The estimation of the population of large bodies is the topic of ongoing research in planet formation. In fact, the evolution of the streaming instability power law initial mass function (IMF) is yet under study. However, some research on pebble and planetesimal accretion suggests that the IMF becomes shallower for larger bodies due to accretion. A slope of α l = 0.14 was estimated for such distribution, implying an upper limit of about 1000 bodies with H r < 2 (dwarf planet size bodies). Nevertheless, such estimation turns out to be clearly smaller than the requirement of up to 4000 large bodies necessary for the grainy Neptune migration mechanism. Here, we adopt a slightly steeper slope (α l = 0.18) at large size range so that grainy migration is preserved and dynamical depletion allows for the right number of dwarf planets currently observed in the Kuiper belt. Therefore, the cumulative SFD for the inner disc is obtained as the combination of an exponential taper function and a power law for bodies larger than D tr. The resulting function is as follows:

N(<H r) = N i1 10^α s (H r − H 0) exp [−10^β(H r − H B)] + N i2 10^α l (H r − H 0) (4)

In order to obtain the SFD in the hot population, we assume an albedo of p r = 0.08, representative of such population. Figure 3b shows the initial SFDs tested in this study for the cold population and the inner region for D tr = 100 km. Simply grafting the SFDs for bodies larger and smaller than D tr does not provide a suitable match to the observed populations when evolved. Instead, summing up the taper and the power law (Fig. 3b), leads to a distribution that provides an excellent agreement between the observed and modelled populations. We test D tr values of 100 and 400 km to look for the best fit to observables. We also test a shallower SFD initial slope (α s = 0.3) for small-size bodies, but in this case, collisional evolution is not able to rebuild the population to the currently estimated SFD.

Impact velocity and intrinsic probability
Abedin et al. estimated that impacts between KBOs can currently happen over a wide range of relative velocities, mostly well below 5 km/s, in agreement with previous estimates. Therefore, we assume a Maxwellian relative velocity distribution around the most probable value (v p) for each modelled population. v p is adjusted to the dynamical conditions governed by eccentricity and inclination at each time step for each population. Collisional probabilities are calculated accordingly, taking into account the corresponding intrinsic collisional probability P int. The intrinsic collisional probability of bodies occupying a given volume depends on the average relative velocity and the volume itself. The average relative velocity can be calculated as a function of the average orbital eccentricity and inclination of the system (v rel / sqrt(e^2 + sin^2 i)), while the volume depends on the range of orbital inclinations and the boundary orbital semi-major axes (see Table 1).

Figure 4 shows the change in v p and P int for the inner disc along phases 1 and 2, corresponding to t i = 10, 30, 50, and 100 Myr. In the outer disc, we assume that once bodies are implanted into the Plutinos and HKB regions, they do not change their orbit elements any longer. Thus, the most probable values of the impact velocity and the mean intrinsic probability for that zone are constant. The cold population increases its inclination during phase 1, implying an increase in v p and decrease in P int. The values of v p and P int for each KB population are listed in Table 2.

Time dependence
Dynamical models give a rough estimate of when the dynamical instability started (t i). In previous studies the dependence of the evolution on the onset of dynamical instability was searched for, reaching up to 700 Myr. In this new approach, based on an early onset, we test t i = 10, 20, 30, 50, and 100 Myr. The nominal duration of the instability time interval, Δt, is set at 10 Myr as a nominal value, but we also explore longer instability time spans up to Δt = 30 Myr, without significant changes in the final distribution. For all runs in this section, we consider the weakest scaling law.

Collisional evolution is limited for two main reasons in this system. On the one hand, as described by dynamical models, the mass of the inner belt has to be reduced to 20 M⊕ by the onset of dynamical instability. On the other hand, the characteristic initial SFD concentrates most of the mass in large bodies (D > 100 km), lowering collisional probabilities.

We explore the effect on the SFD of assuming different values for such onset time, and we find that delaying the onset of instability from 10 to 100 Myr has the only effect of slightly increasing collisional evolution, causing a dip around 10 km (from 3 to 30 km, approximately). In this case, the wavy pattern triggered at small sizes has enough time to extend to larger sizes (Fig. 5). However, no reliable observational evidence for the existence of such dip is currently available, but cannot be completely ruled out, as it lies below observational completeness (about 100 km).

Figure 6 shows changes in mass over time, due to collisional and dynamical effects, giving a snapshot of the outcome associated with varying the onset of the dynamic instability. Our results show that the later the dynamical instability sets in, the more significant the mass fraction lost by collisional grinding. For instance, if instability occurs early, at 10 Myr, only 2% of the primordial mass is lost due to collisions, but if it is delayed until 100 Myr, mass loss may be as high as 15%.

Model flexibility to match observational uncertainties
In this section, we explore the threshold values of the parameters that define the initial distribution, producing an evolved population consistent with observational uncertainties. It is worth mentioning that, for completeness, we also explore the uncertainty range in the SFD at large sizes provided by the OSSOS++ project. Equation (3) defines the initial cold population, characterised by the parameters N c1, α s, and β. Following eq. (4), the parameters for the inner population are N i1, N i2, α s, β, and α l. Our methodology for constructing the initial distribution begins with the cold population. The α s parameter was constrained using the error band for the debiased estimation for the three detections by Bernstein et al. in the cold population (approximately at 15 km). The β parameter was constrained using OSSOS++ uncertainties at large sizes, where these are more significant. Eventually, the normalization parameter N c1 needed adjustment. Then, we build the initial distribution for the inner zone population. Here, the premise is to keep the slopes of the exponential taper component (α s, β) constant, established in the previous step, leaving N i1 and the parameters defining the power law component (α l and N i2) as free parameters. N i1 and N i2 are fixed to ensure the primordial distribution starts with about 30 M⊕, keeping the number of dwarf planets consistent with the grainy migration scenario. In order to limit the number of simulations in this section, the scaling law is set as the one corresponding to the most fragile objects, and t i = 30 Myr.

Figure 7a illustrates the initial SFD in the inner belt and the evolved SFD in the hot population. The shallow beta (0.23) requires a steeper slope (α l = 0.45) of the power law contribution for the evolved HKB distribution to match the upper OSSOS++ uncertainty at larger sizes. Contrarily, steeper β requires a shallower power law slope to match the lower OSSOS++ uncertainty. Figure 7b shows the initial and evolved SFD for the cold population. OSSOS++ uncertainties at larger sizes require 0.23 < β < 0.3. Thus, a narrow range for each parameter is allowable to commit the observational uncertainties for the CKB. For reference, the best fit is achieved for α s = 0.4 and β = 0.3, closer to the upper threshold values.

For all the runs listed in Table 3, primordial mass in Pluto-class objects (D > 1800 km) is between 18 and 40% of the initial mass contained between about 1900 and 6000 bodies, in agreement with the grainy migration requirement. Furthermore, mass in bodies larger than 100 km is in the range of about 47–88%. According to our best fit, after 4500 Myr of dynamical and collisional evolution, the Poisson probability of having at least one Pluto-class object in the plutinos population is 0.73. The probability of having at least two dwarf planets (D > 1400 km) in the HKB is 0.80.

A deeper statistical analysis, such as a Bayesian MCMC approach, could be useful in the context of a more detailed investigation, which lies beyond the scope of this work. This method would allow for a probabilistic exploration of the parameter space, making it particularly valuable for population matching within specific size ranges, where more precise estimations of the number of bodies could be directly compared with modelling results.

Review of NCOMMS-23-32884
The authors present a concise description of some collisional evolution simulations that they have done which simultaneously accounts for the varied dynamical history of the proto Kuiper Belt. The outputs of their simulations produce size distributions which broadly match observations presented by Petit et al.
The authors make a bold claim that they simultaneously reproduce the size distributions of both the cold classical and dynamically excited populations. This is a disingenuous claim that oversells what they have actually found. Such a result is exactly what is to be expected given the input dynamics and the shattering model they have chosen, so as to be broadly compatible with other observations such as the pluto cratering record. That is to say, little evolution is expected for the cold population, and by nature of their adopted strength model, similar results are expected for the hot population. They haven't started from a vastly different size distribution that converges on the current. Their result is better stated that the features in the current size distributions of both populations that match expectations from the streaming instability model are preserved given expectations from the dynamics we know to have occurred, and with an appropriately chosen strength model. This is a much more truthful - and much less exciting - result than what they claim. At best, they have put together the pieces, and got out exactly what one would expect.
The authors also make the claim that they start with the same size distribution for both populations, and end up with matches to the current observations. This isn't actually true, as they require that the hot distribution start with a power law feature for large bodies that doesn't exist in the cold population. If they had actually created this feature from a common starting point, that would be a very exciting result, but instead they arbitrarily adopt a curve that matches current observations without any physical justification, but is required as their model doesn't naturally reproduce it. Nor should it as this feature looks accretional in nature rather than destructive. They simply do not start from the same place as the authors state.
The authors make no effort to admit the uncertainties in the observed size distribution, but rather only present the nominal measurement. This hides a property of their initial size distribution - it is already within the uncertainty curve quoted by Petit et al for the cold population, and is no further away from the observation than the final outputs of their simulation. Their initial curve would match the observations just as well as the final result, but with no evolution what so ever.
There is a potentially interesting result that the authors do not discuss, which also forms the basis of their calculations. Namely the strength scaling laws they require that differ significantly from those of a decade ago. This is a critical piece of their calculations, and cannot be presented in an unreadable future publication, but rather absolutely must be presented and justified here.
Finally, they seem to avoid one of the interesting results they have come up with, where the simulated distribution of the hot population is incompatible with previous size distribution efforts derived from the pluto cratering record. Rather than address this interesting result, they decide to punt to a presumably future effort.

The authors have done a decent job in altering the claims in the manuscript to reflect what they have found from their simulations. They have also improved the presentation of the modelling, and the assumptions made therein. In that sense, the paper presents a lot better and lot more complete than the original version.
I still have numerous significant concerns however that have not been addressed:
1. The authors have failed to include a robust discussion of uncertainties. This goes two ways. Observationally, the data they are matching their models against (the OSSOS results) have significant uncertainties regarding detection rates that the authors do not make any use of. I have checked with Petit and Kavelaars and their publications and the uncertainties are available their, or through an email (which it seems the authors must have done at some point already).
Similarly there is no robust analysis of numerical uncertainties, most importantly the effects of model assumptions on the outputs. They have done a better job of discussing this, but only present a few models, which is hardly a complete discussion.
The major outstanding question is how far can the nominal model be bent and still be consistent with the range of possible SFDs allowable by the OSSOS data?
The above question immediately reflects upon whether or not the author's simulation outputs are common to a large range of possible models, or require very particular assumptions to get it "just right". Either scenario would be interesting, but as it stands, the reader cannot currently know this.
2. Similarly to point 1 above, FIgure 3 has data points with no uncertainties, and curves with no uncertainties, which makes the presentation disingenuous. Given the uncertainties on the crater counts, it is reasonable to expect that a number of different models could be made to fit the possible range of crater count values, not just the singular model they argue for.
3. I didn't raise this issue with the first review because it was already too long, so I raise it here. There are numerous other sources of measurement the authors have not considered. In particular the Bernstein 2004 result which presents the smallest size objects for which a direct SFD can be measured. Similarly, the bright end can be further constrained with the MPC dataset which is mostly complete at sizes larger than the OSSOS upper size range. Both of these results must be matched for the model to stand. Even an approximate match in the way done in Kavelaars 2021 would be sufficient, and so this shouldn't take too much effort.

Reasonable estimates of the number of H<8.3 objects predict an oder of magnitude more objects in that size range than the entire known sample. We provide a few here:
From the early works of Gladman, Jewitt, Fraser, Fuentes, and Jones, the apparent magnitude distribution has slope alpha~0.7. review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Understanding how the observed size distribution of Kuiper Belt objects emerged from the primordial planetesimal population remains a major challenge in planetary science. In particular, the similarity between the size distributions of dynamically hot and cold populations in the 100–400 km range calls for a unified explanation. Motivated by this observational constraint and by theoretical models of pebble accretion, we model the coupled dynamical and collisional evolution of the trans-planetary disc under the early instability scenario. Here we show that a common planetesimal formation mechanism operating up to about 400 km and modulated by an exponential taper shape, combined with a transition to a shallow power law distribution in the inner disc, can reproduce the current size-frequency distributions of cold and hot populations. This outcome requires assuming that planetesimals were weaker to impacts than previously thought. Our results connect formation models with current observations, thereby constraining the early conditions of the Solar System and the properties of planetesimals.

---

## Introduction

The inventory of dynamically hot and cold Kuiper belt objects (KBOs) has been proposed to be nearly complete for objects with absolute magnitude H r < 5.3, and this has been confirmed by dedicated surveys. The achievement of near completeness in that magnitude range opens new possibilities to better constrain the early Solar System after the gas dispersal phase.

The Outer Solar System Origins Survey (OSSOS), along with following extensions referred to as OSSOS++, provides a comprehensive debiased sample of dynamically hot and cold Kuiper belt (KB) populations (hereinafter HKB and CKB, respectively), together with their absolute magnitude H r distribution. Supported by such surveys, the H r distribution of the cold classical population was found to be accurately approximated by an exponentially tapered function in H r ≃ 5 to 12 range. Later findings indicate that the absolute magnitude distributions of dynamically hot and cold populations in the 5.5 < H r < 8.3 range (corresponding roughly to 100–400 km diameter range) are essentially indistinguishable. Such observational evidence provided by OSSOS++ contradicts the previously prevailing view, when it was widely accepted that the cumulative size-frequency distributions (SFD) of the hot and cold components of the KB were well described by broken power laws of the form N(>D) ∝ Dq, where N(>D) is the number of objects with diameter larger than D, and q is the cumulative slope of the distribution. Specifically, at the large-size end (D > 100 km), the cold component was thought to have a steeper slope (q cold = −7.5) than the hot component (q hot = −4.5). The evidence provided by has posed a challenge to the previous notion that the primordial Kuiper belt displayed different SFDs slopes in its inner and outer regions, implying different formation processes.

The general understanding of the outer solar system dynamical evolution is encompassed under the umbrella of the new Nice model. According to this model, the planetesimals surrounding the giant planets, remaining after their formation, were located in a disc extending about 22 to 30 au, with an estimated mass about 30 M⊕. As dynamical instability ensued, the influence of Neptune played a significant role in depleting that disc. Most of the mass was dispersed at very large heliocentric distance, while some bodies were implanted in the current region of Plutinos, and others eventually found their way to the HKB.

There is a consensus on the hypothesis that the cold population, with a current mass of about 10−3 M⊕, was born in situ and remained primordial, based on the large fraction of binaries still in the CKB and their distinctive red colours. This argument was later reinforced by the New Horizons images of Arrokoth, showing scarcity of craters on its surface, suggesting that collisional evolution did not significantly alter the primordial SFD of that population. Based on measurements by OSSOS++, it has been suggested that the SFD of the cold and hot components may have maintained their primordial shape for objects in the size range of about 100–400 km. Accordingly, the same mechanism responsible for the accretion of bodies in their primordial formation region might be common to both populations.

As far as planetesimal growth is concerned, the streaming instability (SI) model gives valuable insights into the initial phase of planetesimal formation by providing an efficient and fast mechanism for growing planetesimals from dust particles or pebble clumps within protoplanetary discs. The SI is an aerodynamic process driven by the velocity difference between solid particles and gas and the reaction of solids onto the gas. This mechanism led to the formation of high-density regions, providing a favourable environment for gravitational collapse and subsequent aggregation into planetesimals.

Lyra et al. found that considering a pebble size distribution in the accretion process (also refereed as polydisperse pebble accretion) following SI was critical in planetesimal formation. According to this study, such a process was responsible for accretion of up to a few hundred km (about 300–400 km) at heliocentric distances as far as the current location of the CKB. This finding is essential in defining a common formation mechanism for the primordial trans–planetary populations (between 22 and 30 au) and the cold population of bodies up to such size, confirming previous conjectures. According to accretion models, further growth strongly depends on mass conditions at different heliocentric distances. This is the reason why accretion to Pluto (and possibly larger) size bodies was efficient in the inner region between 22 and 30 au. Instead, beyond 40 au, planetesimals should have remained as such, as further accretion was prevented by low mass density conditions in the nebula.

The inventory of large bodies in the Kuiper belt seems nowadays relatively complete for H r < 5.3, while the SFD of fainter (smaller) bodies remains largely incomplete. Valuable insights into impactor SFD and collisional processes are achieved by exploring planetary surface impact craters. Thus, the surfaces of Pluto and Charon offer a unique opportunity to examine the crater population in the outer solar system. Robins et al. provide results that reconcile earlier discrepancies in the estimated crater size distribution slopes obtained from the New Horizons fly-by of both worlds. They estimate that the size distribution of small craters has a shallower slope than for large ones, consistent with previously reported results by Singer et al. (hereinafter S19). Nevertheless, according to the authors, the crater size-frequency distribution slopes are uncertain, in particular at small sizes. In fact, slope values for craters below 10–15 km is −0.7 ± 0.2, and −2.8 ± 0.6 for larger craters; implying a deficit of small KBOs below 1–2 km. Such estimated slopes are very sensitive to the choice of parameters and the craters used in the statistical analysis, and they must be taken as minima in the uncertainty determination. On the other hand, Morbidelli et al. (hereinafter M21) established a connection between their re-examined Pluto and Charon cratering record and Arrokoth’s cratering record, including the dust measurement (down to 2 μm approximately) obtained from the New Horizons space mission by NASA. Their findings revealed that the SFD shows a moderate decline below 2 km, which contrasts with the claim made by S19 of an exceedingly shallow slope. In addition, M21 argue that the shallow portion of the SFD extends to around 30 m before transitioning to a steeper slope to match the dust abundance constraint.

Collisional models are commonly used to study small body populations evolution in the solar system. However, since the adoption of the new Nice model framework, only two studies have examined the collisional evolution of the trans-planetary disc in detail. First, Asteroid-LIke Collisional And Dynamical Evolution Package (ALICANDEP-22) was applied to conduct a systematic study exploring different initial distributions for the trans–planetary disc and different scaling laws that govern the impact response. They got a good match with available observational evidence when it was still thought that the CKB and HKB had different SFD slopes at the bright end. Later, the Boulder code was applied to study the collisional evolution of the primordial KB and other related populations as the destabilised population and the Jupiter Trojans. The main constraints used in the latter include the size distributions of the Trojan asteroids and craters on the giant planets satellites.

The presence of Pluto-sized and larger bodies in the hot population implies that the initial SFD of the inner trans-planetary disc must have extended beyond 400 km. Moreover, theoretical studies of planetesimal accretion suggest that, in the inner disc, a power law tail likely developed with a relatively shallow slope, enabling the growth of several thousand dwarf planets. When combined with an exponentially tapered distribution, characteristic of the cold population, this configuration provides a natural explanation for the properties of the hot and cold Kuiper Belt populations within a unified formation framework.

Here we show that the observed SFDs of both dynamically hot and cold Kuiper Belt populations can be reproduced by modelling their collisional and dynamical evolution from a common primordial distribution. We adopt an initial SFD shaped by a shared formation mechanism up to 400 km, transitioning to a shallow power law tail in the inner disc, and evolve it under the early instability scenario. Our simulations indicate that matching current observations requires assuming low material strength for planetesimals.

---

## Results

Outline of the model
We modelled the KB collisional and dynamical evolution using the ALICANDEP-22 package. This model simulates collisional evolution within the framework of the current interpretation of the Nice model for the dynamical evolution of the outer solar system. Dynamical evolution is carried out through statistical elimination of bodies from an inner disc and implantation into the current KB. The modelled scenario begins with the initial mass concentrated in an inner disc (outside Neptune’s orbit), ranging from 22 to 30 au. We also considered a small concentration of mass between 42 and 47 au, standing for the in-situ formation of the cold classical population. The initial population born in the inner disc undergoes three evolution phases, including collisional and dynamical evolution processes such as excitation, migration, and mass depletion. Each phase consists of the following features. Phase 1: We call this the pre-instability phase, lasting from time t 0 to t i. It denotes the onset of Neptune’s outward migration as it enters the inner disc. This phase results in an increase in eccentricity and inclination of planetesimals. Such dynamical excitation increased relative velocities (see “Methods”) and, therefore, the overall collisional evolution. Additionally, some smooth mass-loss during this period—according to dynamical models—is also included. Phase 2: This period is known as the instability phase. In our model, it lasts from t i to t i + Δt. In this phase, Neptune passed through the inner disc, which led to minor collisional evolution and significant dynamical depletion. During this time, most planetesimals were ejected from the solar system; some were removed inwards, while others were implanted into the excited Kuiper belt populations. Phase 3: This is the post-instability phase, lasting from t i + Δt to the end of the simulations (4500 Myr). At the beginning of this phase, the inner disc was already depleted, and the outer regions corresponding to Plutinos and hot classical belt populations were populated. Negligible collisional evolution took place in this phase.

In ALICANDEP-22, the outer region of the solar system is divided into three zones, representing different Kuiper belt populations: Plutinos, cold classicals, and hot classicals. The collisional evolution of each zone is performed taking into account mutual interaction between different zones. The orbital elements, semi-major axis (a), eccentricity (e) and inclination (i) of the inner zone and the three outer zones for each dynamical phase, are shown in Table 1. For the instability onset we tested t i = 10 to 100 Myr, with Δt = 10 and 30 Myr.

Regarding the response of bodies to impacts, numerical studies tend to shift from 200 m to around 20 m, the size at which scaling laws for the threshold specific energy for disruption (Q* D) have a minimum. This was first suggested to suitably fit the cratering record on Pluto, Charon, and Arrokoth, and to explain the survival of the satellite of the Trojan asteroid Eurybates (Queta). Moreover, a study on collisional evolution of the primordial Kuiper belt, its destabilised population, and the Trojans asteroids, also finds that such scaling laws produce better results to match the Trojan asteroids populations and the crater distributions on giant planets satellites. Further details about the implementation of scaling laws are presented in the Methods section.

The initial SFD is an essential boundary condition in the progress of populations of systems under moderate collisional evolution. In such systems, as in the case of the Kuiper belt, the SFD slopes for large bodies are not modified along the evolution; thus, their features must be primordial. Accordingly, we must reproduce the gradual transition towards larger bodies currently observed in the SFD of the implanted hot component. Therefore, we propose that the initial population in the inner trans–planetary region combines a tapered distribution up to D tr about 100–400 km, with a decreasing power law distribution for D > D tr. Such population contained around of 4000 Pluto–size (and larger) bodies. Two values were tested for D tr: 100 and 400 km. In the case of the primordial cold disc, an SFD identical in shape to the inner disc but with much less mass—and no population of bodies larger than 400 km—was chosen as the initial distribution, following the planetesimal formation mechanisms discussed above. At the small-size end, the cumulative H r magnitude distribution is governed by an exponent α s (see “Methods,” subsection Initial size distribution). In the following section, we show results for primordial distributions with α s values of 0.4 and 0.3, which are our steep and shallow distributions (see “Methods,” subsection Model flexibility to match observational uncertainties, for a detailed exploration of the initial SFD parameters). The total mass of the primordial population is approximately 30 M⊕, assuming an average bulk density of 1000 kg/m3.

Observational constraints
The main constraint in this study comes from the debiased magnitude distribution of the hot and cold populations provided by updated surveys. The OSSOS++ team graciously provided us with the magnitude distribution of each component, making this task easier. Due to the fact that the OSSOS++ survey may overestimate the size distribution of bright bodies, we preferred to use the Minor Planet Center (MPC) database for the distribution of bodies with H r ≲ 5.5. Several pencil-beam surveys have been conducted to identify faint Kuiper belt objects. Bernstein et al. used the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to measure the faintest Kuiper belt objects for which a direct SFD can be obtained. They detected three CKB bodies and none in the HKB population. Kavelaars et al. debiased the three detections in the cold population using the same procedure as for OSSOS++. This estimation is also used in this work as an observational constraint. In the Methods section, we utilize observational uncertainties to investigate the flexibility of the model while ensuring it remains consistent with the range of possible SFD permitted by the OSSOS++ data, including the debiased estimation by Bernstein et al.

We assumed the average albedo of each population (p r = 0.15 and 0.08 for cold and hot KBOs, respectively) for size conversion. Both tested transition sizes D tr = 100 and 400 km provide satisfactory results; however, we centred our analysis on the case corresponding to D tr = 100 km, because it best matched the constraint of a smooth slope transition in the 100–400 km size range to larger bodies. In the subsection Considerations on the Kuiper Belt Populations, two additional constraints are discussed: the change in the SFD slope at 1–2 km and the Jupiter trojans SFD slope for 5–100 km size bodies.

Model outcome
Figure 1 shows the model outcome of the cumulative SFD for the hot and cold populations after 4500 Myr of evolution. For comparison, the SFD corresponding to the debiased absolute magnitude distribution for each dynamical population is also shown along with the corresponding Poisson 95% confidence range estimated by the OSSOS++. Different scaling laws were tested, showing that the final distributions, for large bodies, are not very sensitive to the very values of the scaling law for shattering (Q* S), provided that we choose a weak one and that the minimum value of the distribution is about 20 m (see “Methods,” subsection Impact outcome).

Hot classical population
The match between the modelled hot classical population and the debiased distribution is excellent, particularly in the size range from about 70 to 400 km. For larger bodies, the modelled SFD follows the MPC database, essentially complete at this size range. Nevertheless, for completeness, we also explore the uncertainty range of the OSSOS++ survey (see Methods, subsection Model flexibility to match observational uncertainties).

The hot classical population was born in a massive disc, though with low relative velocities due to small values of eccentricity and inclination. That circumstance only allowed fair collisional grinding down to about 20 km. However, at sizes below 100 km, a moderate wavy behaviour in the SFD can be noticed, in the case where the weakest scaling law is assumed (solid blue line in Fig. 1a). Collisional grinding appears then subtle, and the very characteristics of each fragmentation scaling law leave minor fingerprints in the evolved SFD, even when delaying the onset of instability from 10 to 100 Myr (see Methods, subsection Time dependence). The shift of the minima in the scaling laws down to some 20 m is crucial in the propagation of the wavy pattern, even at large sizes (about 10 km).

Cold classical population
Agreement of our results with the debiased distribution is very accurate for the cold component across the comparable size range (70 < D < 400 km). That is particularly evident when the assumed initial distribution has a steep slope at the small–size end (α s = 0.4), as is observed today. Further simulations constrain the possible values of α s in the range of 0.27 to 0.42 to be consistent with the error bar of the debiased estimation of the faintest detected objects in the CKB (black error bar in Fig. 1b). The uncertainties of the OSSOS++ also allow a modest variation in the slope of the taper function at large sizes. The threshold values defining the initial SFD are explored in the Methods section.

Negligible collisional evolution took place in this region, and the final distribution is a slightly depleted version of the primordial one. ALICANDEP-22 can keep track of the amount of objects that are disrupted, or just shattered and gravitationally re-aggregated. In this way, we find that—in the cold classical population—bodies larger than about 1–10 km are expected to be primordial and to have experienced only cratering events, even in the case the weakest shattering scaling law is considered in our model. Consequently, their dynamically relaxed initial conditions strongly support that this population was preserved in its primordial state due to negligible collisional evolution. This confirms findings indicating that Arrokoth is most likely a primordial body.

Considerations on the Kuiper Belt populations
It has been pointed out in the literature that the KBO SFD exhibits distinctive features. First, a break at 100 km referred to as the “knee” was found, where the cumulative slope transitions from steeper to shallower. Also, a secondary break at about D = 1–2 km, known as the “elbow,” was suggested, where the slope shifts from a value in the range of −2.8 to −3.2 to an even shallower slope with a corresponding q in the range of −0.7 to −1.2, in terms of cumulative distribution (see Introduction). We find that an exponential taper shape SFD of the primordial population, below 100–400 km, easily reproduces the knee at about 100 km, as shown in Fig. 1, for the hot and cold dynamical population, and in Fig. 2 for the total KB population (Plutinos, HKB, and CKB).

The transition region between the knee and the elbow (2 < D < 100 km) must follow a cumulative SFD slope similar to the one observed in the captured population of Jupiter Trojans (q ~ −2), described by the red dotted line in Fig. 2. We faithfully reproduce such behaviour in all the simulations adopting a steep slope (α s = 0.4) for the current H magnitude distribution. In contrast, beginning the evolution with a shallower slope (α s = 0.3), implies that the final SFD will also be shallower than expected in that transition size range. This is due to the fact that collisional evolution is unable to increase the slope to the one expected for Jupiter Trojans. We show this in Fig. 2, highlighting the need for the chosen slope (α s = 0.4) to meet observational constraints.

The behaviour of the SFD in the vicinity of the elbow deserves closer examination. Following previous studies on crater counts on Pluto and Charon, we consider the impact record estimated for Vulcan Planitia on Charon in S19, as it may best represent the primary population of impactors. Therefore, we obtained the nominal impactor SFD and plotted it along with the outcome of our model (Fig. 2) by suitably scaling it to the Kuiper belt distribution.

The model that best agrees with the predicted impactor population of cratering record estimations features a steep initial slope (α s = 0.4) and the weakest scaling law. This is represented by the solid blue line in Fig. 2. The match is remarkable in the 0.7–10 km size range, approximately. The S19 impactor distribution at smaller sizes instead bends over along a shallower slope. There is limited data availability in the sub-kilometer size range, so uncertainties related to crater count are relevant. Figure 2b shows the elbow size range in detail, including uncertainty estimation within 2σ (for small bodies), using as a reference the number of impactors corresponding to about D = 1.5 km, where the distribution gradually changes its slope. Our best matching case reproduces fairly well the gradual slope change (between 1 and 2 km) confirmed by crater count, while for smaller bodies it is close to the upper 2σ slope uncertainty, for the estimated distribution of impactors. For completeness, the cumulative distribution estimated by M21 is also plotted in Fig. 2b. The slope of the SFD corresponding to M21 model is similar to that found in our study in the 0.1–1 km size range, except for their underestimated population (by a factor about 3) below 1 km. Given the uncertainties in slope estimation of the crater size distribution, mainly due to the smooth transition from large to small craters, S19 and M21 estimations are not necessarily at odds with each other, and our model seem to be compatible with both interpretations within uncertainty limits.

In any case, we find that the only way to reproduce the elbow is to assume a weak strength for bodies in the primordial trans–planetary disc. This finding is in agreement with the 2023 study by Bottke et al. of collisional evolution based on current Trojan asteroids SFD and giant planets satellites cratering data, requiring a similar scaling law to be matched. Thus, despite the relatively small influence of collisional evolution, restricted to an early phase and constrained by the onset of the early solar system dynamical depletion, it is still significant in producing a bump at 1–2 km and propagating the wavy shape up to 10 km in the evolved SFD. Observational efforts are imperative for improving our comprehension of sub-kilometre outer solar system bodies and refining our understanding of the distinctive features characterising such population.

While the SFD estimated by M21 broadly corresponds to our overall final SFD in the approximate size range of 2–100 km, differences show up at smaller sizes, particularly around 30 m, where the slope turns steep in M21. In our model, the transition to a steep slope occurs at about 100 m, rather than at 30 m. Therefore, M21 underestimate the total number of bodies in the 10−2 < D < 1 km range, compared to our results. At the smallest size end (D < 10−3 km), both models tend to converge to the steady state slope. An explanation for such discrepancy may be that their estimation of the total SFD is derived from the impact cratering record of bodies associated with different dynamical populations, such as Pluto and Charon (in the plutinos 3:2 mean motion resonance region), and Arrokoth (CKB). The key difference in our model, compared to M21’s, is the ability to follow the collisional evolution of individual populations, including their mutual interactions, resulting in accurate outcome of the end–state overall populations.
